questions.q:
Identify the segment in the sentence which contains a grammatical error.

The teacher evaluates students not only on his performance in exams but also on their participation in class discussions.
o: not only on his performance
in exams but also on their
questions.s:
The erroneous part is '​not only on his performance'.

Key Points

  • The error in this sentence lies in the use of the possessive pronoun "his" to refer to the plural noun "students." The correct possessive pronoun for the plural noun "students" should be "their" for agreement in number.
    • Corrected sentence: "The teacher evaluates students not only on their performance in exams but also on their participation in class discussions."
  • In the original sentence, "The teacher evaluates students not only on his performance in exams but also on their participation in class discussions," the use of "his" is incorrect because it refers to the singular possessive form, which does not agree in number with the plural noun "students." This inconsistency creates a lack of agreement between the pronoun and the noun it's referencing.
  • The correction replaces "his" with "their" to maintain agreement in number. "Their" is the plural possessive pronoun that correctly corresponds to the plural noun "students." This adjustment ensures grammatical accuracy by having the pronoun match the plural subject in terms of number.

questions.q:
The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.

A tiger’s skull / is similar / to / a lion.
questions.s:
The erroneous part is: a lion.

Key Points

  • The word "lion" should be replaced with "lion's" to make the sentence grammatically correct.
  • The sentence contains a subject ("A tiger’s skull") and a predicate ("is similar to a lion").
  • When we use the structure "is similar to," we are making a comparison between two entities.
  • The key point here is that we are comparing the tiger's skull to the lion's skull (implied), not just the animal itself.
  • In other words, we need to show that we are comparing the skull of a tiger to the skull of a lion, rather than comparing the skull to the whole lion.
  • To express the possession of the skull by the lion, we need to use the possessive form of the noun "lion." This is done by adding an apostrophe and "s" to "lion," making it "lion's."

Hence, the correct answer is: a lion's.
